passage: Lunch-break note, Ms Alka. I noticed Bhupen at the end of the bench with no tiffin today. His friend Yash slid his own box towards him. "Mum packed too much," Yash said, and carried on talking about cricket as if nothing had happened. Bhupen's ears went pink and he stared at the box. He said, "Thanks," softly, took one piece of paratha, and smiled a small, awkward smile. I stayed at my desk and did not step in. The next day Bhupen came with roasted chana in a twist of paper. "Have some," he said. Yash took a big handful and said it was tasty. Both boys looked pleased.

qa.q: What did Bhupen bring the next day?
qa.a: He brought roasted chana in a twist of paper.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling when his ears went pink and he stared at the box?
qa.a: Probably awkward and embarrassed at being helped, along with gratitude, since he thanked Yash softly and smiled a small smile.

qa.q: What made it easier for Bhupen to accept Yash's food?
qa.a: Yash did not make a show of it and kept talking about cricket, so Bhupen could accept warmly and later share something of his own. 😊

qa.q: How might Yash have seen the moment when he slid his box over?
qa.a: As something ordinary, since he said Mum packed too much and carried on talking about cricket.

grounding: A child gratefully but awkwardly accepts a richer friend's tiffin and shares something of his own in return.

passage:
In the school lunch hall, Aparna opened her steel box: two dry rotis and a pinch of salt. It had been a tight month at home. She angled the lid so nobody could see.
Abhinav slid into the seat beside her with his three-tier tiffin. Without a word, he pushed the middle tier, paneer and peas, halfway between them and began eating from his side as if that were normal.
Aparna's cheeks warmed. She felt thankful and a bit awkward all at once. Was it pity? But Abhinav was only talking about the cricket match, not looking at her rotis at all.
"Thanks," she said quietly, and tore a roti to share with him.
The next day she brought guavas from the tree behind her house, salted and cut, and put the best half on his lid.

qa.q: What was in the middle tier Abhinav shared?
What did Aparna feel when Abhinav pushed the tier over?
qa.a: Grateful and a bit awkward at the same time, wondering whether it was pity.

qa.q: How did Aparna respond in a way that kept the friendship equal?
qa.a: She accepted warmly, shared her roti, and the next day brought guavas to share with him.

qa.q: How does Abhinav seem to see sharing his tiffin?
qa.a: As something normal between friends, not a favour; he made no show of it.

grounding: A girl whose richer friend shares his tiffin without fuss feels grateful and awkward, accepts warmly and shares something of her own.

passage:
Monday: Rafiq's lunch was a single bun; Abbu's rickshaw had broken down again. His friend Kartik, whose family owned the sweet shop, quietly tore his big cheese sandwich in two and put half on Rafiq's napkin. "Too much for me." He didn't look at the bun at all. Rafiq said thanks, but his neck felt hot.
Tuesday: Kartik did it again. This time Rafiq pushed it back. "I'm not hungry." His stomach growled loudly. Kartik shrugged, but looked a little hurt.
Thursday: The night before, Rafiq had rolled extra shami kebabs with Ammi and his sister Ishita. At lunch he opened his box and pushed it to the middle. "Ammi's kebabs. Your turn to share." Kartik grinned and set his sandwich beside them. They ate from both, trading bites and cricket scores.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq push the sandwich back on Tuesday?
qa.a: He felt awkward and proud, uncomfortable taking help again even though he was hungry.

qa.q: What did Rafiq do on Thursday that made accepting easier?
qa.a: He brought Ammi's kebabs to share, so both boys gave and received.

qa.q: How might Kartik have felt when Rafiq refused on Tuesday?
qa.a: A little hurt, since he was sharing as a friend, not showing off.

grounding: A boy whose richer friend quietly shares his lunch feels grateful but awkward, and learns to accept warmly and share something of his own in return.
